Background (from the session that started this one):
Today (2026-11-16) Kenneth closed the old issues that were about JusPrin v1. He chose to leave issue 12 open because Homebrew support still applies to JusPrin 2. The latest release is at https://github.com/TheSpaghettiDetective/JusPrin/releases/latest. Local jusprin-dev has unpushed commits and Kenneth asked to hold the push, so do not push it.

Task:
Look into GitHub issue 12 on TheSpaghettiDetective/JusPrin, which asks for JusPrin to be installable with Homebrew on macOS. Read the issue and its comments first. Then find out what homebrew-cask needs today to accept a new app: its notability rules for GitHub repositories, signing and notarization, auto-update handling (JusPrin has its own updater, under src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Updates/), and how the release assets are named. Check whether a cask for JusPrin or OrcaSlicer already exists, and copy how the OrcaSlicer cask is written if there is one. The release build is .github/workflows/jusprin_release.yml.

Done means two things. First, a drafted cask file in the scratch directory, tested locally with `brew install --cask ./jusprin.rb`, `brew audit --cask --new` and `brew style`. Second, a short report: whether JusPrin meets the cask rules today, what is missing if it doesn't, and whether submitting to homebrew-cask or running our own tap is the better route. Do not open a pull request on Homebrew, create a tap repository, or post on the issue without Kenneth's yes.

name: JusPrin release

# Builds JusPrin from one commit and uploads the files to a DRAFT GitHub
# release. It never publishes anything.
#
# - The version is the one in src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Updates/Version.hpp, and
#   the draft is tagged jusprin/v<version>, as JusPrin 1.4.0 was (the repo
#   still holds OrcaSlicer's own v2.x tags). GitHub creates that tag only when
#   the draft is published, by hand, on the Releases page. JusPrin's update
#   check reads the public release list, which never includes drafts, so
#   users see nothing until then.
# - It stops if that version is already released, is not above every
#   released JusPrin version, or its tag already exists
#   (Packaging/release.mjs), and if
#   Packaging/release-notes/<version>.md, the notes the draft starts with and
#   that the app shows under "What's new", is missing.
# - It also stops if the guide was not checked for this version
#   (docs/guide/checked-version.txt, written by scripts/check_guide.py
#   --ask-ai; see docs/guide/README.md), unless "Release without the guide
#   check" is ticked. Then the draft's title says the guide was not checked.
# - Running it again for the same version replaces the draft's files.
# - Files: Windows x64 installer and portable zip, macOS universal disk image,
#   Linux x64 AppImage, and SHA256SUMS.txt.
# - Only the release publisher can run it: the repo variable
#   JUSPRIN_RELEASE_PUBLISHER, or kennethjiang when it is unset.
# - Signing: macOS when "sign_macos" is ticked, with the Apple secrets JusPrin
#   1.x used. Windows builds are unsigned. An unsigned draft says so in its
#   title.
#
# Start it from Actions > JusPrin release > Run workflow (the file must also
# be on the default branch for that button), or by pushing a branch named
# jusprin-release/<anything>.

        type: boolean

I drafted a Homebrew cask for JusPrin 2.0.0 and tested it. It installs, uninstalls and passes `brew style`. `brew audit --cask --new` fails on one point only: the JusPrin repository on GitHub is a fork of OrcaSlicer, and the audit rejects forks. Nothing was posted, pushed, or created on GitHub.

**The cask file:** `/private/tmp/claude/claude-502/-Users-kenneth-Projects-JusPrin/2dda01dd-74f2-4361-9528-69ebd36140ba/scratchpad/jusprin.rb`. A copy is in the shared notes folder as `homebrew-jusprin.rb`. It follows the OrcaSlicer cask: same download pattern, GitHub as the homepage, and no `auto_updates`. Homebrew reserves that flag for apps that download and install their own updates, and JusPrin's updater only tells the person a new version exists. The cask also tells Homebrew's version checker to read JusPrin's `jusprin/v…` release tags and skip OrcaSlicer's `v2.x` tags. When I ran that checker, it found 2.0.0.

**Issue 12:** spuder opened it in May 2025 and offered to do the work. It has no comments. No JusPrin cask exists, and no one has tried to submit one.

**How JusPrin does against each rule:**
- **Signing and notarization:** passes. The 2.0.0 DMG is signed by TSD Technology and notarized by Apple, and macOS accepted it when installed through Homebrew. One risk: in `jusprin_release.yml`, signing is a checkbox that starts unticked. An unsigned release would fail Homebrew's checks on its next update.
- **Popularity:** passes. The repository has 245 stars. A cask submitted by anyone needs 75. A cask we submit ourselves counts as self-submitted and needs 225, which we pass only just.
- **Fork:** fails. Homebrew's rules say the popularity numbers count only for the original repository, not for a fork on GitHub. Its maintainers decide forks one by one. In 2023 they merged OrcaSlicer's own first cask despite this same failure, and they have merged others since. A JusPrin submission would depend on a maintainer agreeing.
- **Release file names:** these work as they are. `JusPrin_Mac_universal_V2.0.0.dmg` at the `jusprin/v2.0.0` tag gives a stable download pattern.

**My recommendation (not decided):** submit to the official Homebrew list first. spuder could submit it, since that needs only 75 stars, or we could submit it ourselves. Once it is accepted, Homebrew's bot updates it on every release with no work from us.

If maintainers reject it, our own tap (a GitHub repository holding the cask) is the fallback. It costs more than it seems:
- We would have to update the cask on every release, for example with a step in the release workflow.
- Homebrew 7 now refuses casks from a tap the user hasn't trusted, which I saw while testing. A user would need to run `brew trust` before `brew install`.

**Also found:** jusprin.com and www.jusprin.com are parked domains that someone else owns. The cask uses the GitHub page as its homepage for that reason.

**How I tested:** Homebrew 7 won't install a cask from a plain file path, so I used a temporary tap that existed only on this Mac. I installed into a scratch folder, so `/Applications/JusPrin.app` was not touched. Afterwards I removed the temporary tap and turned off Homebrew's developer mode, which `brew style` had switched on. I did not launch the installed copy, because it shares a bundle ID with your real app. macOS accepting it was the check that mattered.

# Responsible AI Usage

This guide is for maintainers and contributors who use "Artificial Intelligence"/Large Language Model (AI/LLM) tools when working on Homebrew.
It expands on the [AI/LLM usage rules in our Contributing guide](https://github.com/Homebrew/brew/blob/HEAD/CONTRIBUTING.md#artificial-intelligencelarge-language-model-aillm-usage) and the repository's `AGENTS.md` files with the principles we expect you to apply.

AI tools can make you faster.
They can also produce confidently plausible but wrong output.
These guidelines exist to make Homebrew better rather than shifting work and risk onto other maintainers.

## Human in the loop

AI is not responsible for its output: you are responsible for the output of the AI tools you use.
A pull request with your name on it is your work regardless of how much of it an AI wrote.
Every commit must have a human author or `Co-authored-by` co-author: commits attributed only to AI tools are rejected.
You may credit an AI tool alongside them but must still disclose its involvement in the pull request description.

Verify AI output for correctness as you would that of an avatarless GitHub user with no previous contributions.
Read it, run it, test it and make sure you understand it.

Do not ask other humans to review your AI-generated code until you have reviewed it yourself.
This is already a requirement in our [Contributing guide](https://github.com/Homebrew/brew/blob/HEAD/CONTRIBUTING.md#artificial-intelligencelarge-language-model-aillm-usage): you must review all AI/LLM-generated content before asking anyone in Homebrew to review it.

Answer maintainer questions and pull request review comments yourself without using AI/LLM.
Reviewers need to engage directly with the person responsible for the contribution.

As the [pull request template](https://github.com/Homebrew/brew/blob/HEAD/.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md) sets out, disclose when AI was used to generate or assist with a pull request and explain how you verified the changes.

## Trust appropriately

AI tools should not be trusted much more or much less than those of humans.
Treat their output as a fallible first draft.

Verify output: it may be wrong.
Where Homebrew has fast feedback loops, use them.
Run `brew lgtm` (style, typechecking and tests) on every change, and read the diff with `git diff` to keep it small and intentional.

Review code, but don't try to make all of it perfectly match how you would have written it by hand.
Reviewing for correctness, security and maintainability matters far more than reviewing for personal style; our [Prose Style Guidelines](Prose-Style-Guidelines.md) and RuboCop already cover most of the latter.

Review mission-critical code, such as anything touching installation, security, package downloads or the `Formula` and `Cask` DSLs, much more carefully than a one-off script you run locally (which may not need much review at all).

## Use AI to improve AI

For maintainers or regular contributors, when prompting an AI requires repeated corrections and nudges to get Homebrew conventions right, ask it to write or update an `AGENTS.md` file so the next person and the next agent start from a better place.
We already keep instructions in `AGENTS.md` at the repository root.

It's acceptable to do this in the same pull request as your 3rd or later PR.
Don't do this on your first.

## Try things

LLM technologies are changing month by month.
Don't assume a tool you tried last month or last year is still as good or as bad as it was then.

AI use is a new skill and you will be bad at it initially.
Start on areas where the learning curve is lower and the impact is higher, get better and then take on harder problems.
